meta.title: Who really said "Love built on beauty, soon as beauty, dies"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — genuinely John Donne. It's line 27 of his Elegy "The Anagram," a satirical poem praising an ugly woman. First printed 1633; public domain.

meta.ogDescription: Genuinely John Donne — line 27 of his elegy "The Anagram," a mock-praise of an unlovely face. Confirmed in the scholarly text; first printed 1633.

answer.sourceLine: This is a real Donne line — verse 27 of his Elegy II, “The Anagram,” confirmed verbatim in the scholarly text (RPO, from Helen Gardner’s Oxford edition ↗). It was first printed posthumously in his Poems of 1633. The popular web form adds a stray comma (“Love, built on beauty”); Donne’s text has none.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Helen Gardner, ed., The Elegies and the Songs and Sonnets (Oxford, 1965)

source.excerpt:
Love built on beauty, soon as beauty, dies;
Choose this face, changed by no deformities.
trail: The line is placed at Elegy II, “The Anagram,” line 27 by Wikiquote’s sourced Elegies section ↗.
The exact wording and its couplet appear verbatim in the University of Toronto’s Representative Poetry Online ↗, from Helen Gardner’s Oxford edition.
Popular quote sites reproduce it with an added comma — “Love, built on beauty” — as on Goodreads ↗.
source.excerptNote: The couplet as given in the scholarly text. Read in context, it is not a tender aphorism but the punch line of a mock-encomium: Donne is arguing that a plain, unbeautiful woman makes the safer wife, since a love founded on looks perishes when the looks do.

source.rightsNote: “The Anagram” was written in the 1590s and first printed in Donne’s posthumous Poems (1633), so the poem and its wording are firmly in the public domain. The modern scholarly edition used to confirm the text (Gardner, 1965) is itself in copyright, but the couplet it reproduces is Donne’s own words, unchanged since 1633.

author.bio: John Donne was the foremost of the English “metaphysical” poets, prized for knotty wit, audacious conceits and a voice that ranges from the erotic to the devotional. His Elegies and Songs and Sonnets circulated in manuscript from the 1590s and were first collected in print only after his death, in the Poems of 1633. He later took holy orders and rose to be Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, one of the most celebrated preachers of his age.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but mis-read and mis-punctuated
misattribution.intro: Unlike most quotes pinned on famous poets, this one is really theirs. The trouble isn’t the author — it’s the wording and the meaning.

items.why: The widely shared form adds a comma after the first word — “Love, built on beauty, soon as beauty, dies” — as on Goodreads ↗. Donne’s text has no comma there: “Love built on beauty…”

The line is usually served as a wistful truth about love and mortality. In the actual elegy ↗ it is a witty, half-cynical argument for marrying a plain woman — because a love not built on beauty has nothing to lose when beauty fades.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is sound: it really is John Donne, from Elegy II, “The Anagram,” line 27, per Wikiquote ↗ and the Toronto scholarly text ↗.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Stripped of its poem, the line reads as a gentle meditation on love outliving looks. In place, it is far sharper. “The Anagram” is a mock-encomium — a display piece in which Donne playfully praises a woman, Flavia, whose features are catalogued as anything but lovely, and reasons that this is exactly why she makes an ideal, low-risk wife.

The couplet is the argument’s hinge: if love rests on beauty, it dies when beauty does — so “choose this face, changed by no deformities,” a face with no beauty to lose. It is a paradox typical of Donne, closer to a clever debating point than to a sigh.
detailsBody: Donne underscores the practical logic elsewhere in the poem: “For one night’s revels, silk and gold we choose, / But, in long journeys, cloth and leather use.” Beauty is for a night; durability is for a lifetime.
context.pull: A love with nothing to lose when beauty fades — that is Donne’s joke, and his argument.
